title: Headache: Red Flags and Primary Headache Diagnosis

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with headache presenting to the emergency department or primary care: immediate recognition and management of life-threatening secondary headache (subarachnoid haemorrhage, bacterial meningitis and meningoencephalitis, giant cell arteritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma), then diagnosis and drug treatment of migraine, tension-type and cluster headache, using Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocols with named international guidance where the Saudi documents are silent. Adults only.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The MOH Headache Disorder protocol is issued by the MOH General Directorate of Pharmaceutical Care, carries no version or date, and gives no red-flag list, diagnostic criteria, imaging indications or referral criteria; those come from NICE CG150, NICE NG228 and ICHD-3, named in each place.

Several MOH headache table entries are garbled in the extracted text (ibuprofen prescription maximum, cluster verapamil schedule, the pregnancy triptan entry, sumatriptan route in cluster); those entries are left out or marked, and every dose should be checked against the original PDF.

The MOH protocol lists ergotamine and dihydroergotamine for migraine, whereas NICE CG150 advises not to offer ergots; both positions are shown in the comparison table and ergots are not given as a recommended regimen here.

The MOH protocol lists gabapentin up to 1,200 mg per day as level B migraine prophylaxis whereas NICE CG150 advises not to offer gabapentin; both are shown, and the choice belongs to the treating neurologist.

Giant cell arteritis doses come from a news summary of the British Society for Rheumatology guideline and the nimodipine dose from a prescribing-information based monograph; neither is a Saudi or a primary guideline. Bone protection and acid suppression with steroids were not captured.
No Saudi source states the treatment of acute angle-closure glaucoma, so the only action given is same-day ophthalmology referral.
The MOH meningitis protocol gives no cerebrospinal fluid interpretation thresholds, no renal dosing (it defers to the MOH formulary) and no agent or dose for contact prophylaxis.
Paediatric headache and pregnancy-specific prophylaxis were not covered; NICE advises specialist advice for prophylaxis in pregnancy.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Most headaches are primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster); a minority are secondary headaches from conditions such as subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, giant cell arteritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma, which are identified by red flags. A thunderclap headache is a red-flag symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage; computed tomography (CT) of the head is most accurate within 6 hours of onset, and a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is done at least 12 hours after onset if CT is negative after 6 hours. Bacterial meningitis presents with high-grade fever, headache, altered consciousness and meningeal signs; antibiotics must start within the first hour and must not wait for imaging or lumbar puncture. Frequent use of acute headache drugs for 3 months or more can cause medication-overuse headache, which is treated by stopping the overused drugs.
keyMechanisms: Most headaches are primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster); a minority are secondary headaches from conditions such as subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, giant cell arteritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma, which are identified by red flags.

Bacterial meningitis presents with high-grade fever, headache, altered consciousness and meningeal signs; antibiotics must start within the first hour and must not wait for imaging or lumbar puncture.
Frequent use of acute headache drugs for 3 months or more can cause medication-overuse headache, which is treated by stopping the overused drugs.

symptoms: Sudden-onset headache reaching maximum intensity within 5 minutes (thunderclap).
Headache with fever, vomiting, irritability or altered level of consciousness.
Headache triggered by cough, sneezing, exertion or changing posture.
Aura: fully reversible visual, sensory or speech symptoms developing over at least 5 minutes and lasting 5 to 60 minutes.
Throbbing unilateral headache with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound (migraine).
Severe one-sided orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain with tearing, nasal congestion or restlessness (cluster).
Scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms in an older patient (giant cell arteritis; NICE lists symptoms suggesting giant cell arteritis as a red flag).
physicalSigns: Neck stiffness, Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, jolt accentuation of headache (meningitis).
Papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy, focal neurological deficit, cranial nerve deficit, seizures or altered mental status (raised intracranial pressure or intracranial lesion).
Purpura (meningococcal disease: extensive purpura is an intensive care unit admission criterion in the MOH protocol).
Normal neurological examination in uncomplicated migraine or tension-type headache.
redFlags: Sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within 5 minutes (thunderclap): treat as subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded.
Worsening headache with fever, or fever with neck stiffness or altered consciousness: treat as meningitis, antibiotics within 1 hour.
New neurological deficit, new cognitive dysfunction, personality change or impaired level of consciousness.
Headache triggered by cough, valsalva, sneezing or exercise, or orthostatic headache.
Symptoms suggesting giant cell arteritis, or signs of acute narrow-angle glaucoma.
New headache with compromised immunity (for example HIV or immunosuppressant drugs), a history of malignancy, or vomiting without another cause.
Atypical aura: motor weakness, double vision, visual symptoms in only one eye, poor balance or reduced consciousness.
precipitants: Medication overuse (3 months or more of regular acute treatment).
Menstruation (menstrual-related migraine: attacks from 2 days before to 3 days after the start of menstruation in at least 2 of 3 cycles).
Immunocompromise, age over 50, pregnancy, cirrhosis, alcohol misuse, diabetes and other Listeria risk factors (change the empirical antibiotic regimen for meningitis).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Thunderclap onset; blood in the subarachnoid space on non-contrast CT, or xanthochromia on spectrophotometry of cerebrospinal fluid taken at least 12 hours after onset.
Fever, headache, altered consciousness, meningeal signs; confirmed on cerebrospinal fluid white cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture and polymerase chain reaction.
Treated as a medical emergency on suspicion; temporal artery biopsy of at least 1 cm or temporal and axillary artery ultrasound confirm.
At least five attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours with at least two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate or severe, aggravated by activity, plus nausea or vomiting, or photophobia and phonophobia.
Bilateral, pressing or tightening, mild or moderate, not worsened by routine activity, no nausea or vomiting, at most one of photophobia or phonophobia.
Severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, 1 every other day to 8 a day, with ipsilateral autonomic signs or restlessness.
Headache developed or worsened during 3 months or more of regular use of acute headache drugs.

clinicalManagement.title: First minutes: stabilise and screen for life-threatening headache
actions: Airway, breathing and circulation; assess level of consciousness; treat clinical seizures.

Ask: onset within 5 minutes (thunderclap)? Fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness? Head trauma in the past 3 months? New neurological deficit? Immunocompromise or cancer? Age and symptoms of giant cell arteritis? Painful red eye?
Any red flag: do not diagnose a primary headache; follow the matching pathway below.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected bacterial meningitis or meningoencephalitis
actions: Isolate (droplet, airborne and contact precautions if meningococcal disease is suspected); take at least two blood culture sets, then start antibiotics within 1 hour without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture.

Adult under 50, no penicillin allergy: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 4 to 6 hours) plus vancomycin (loading 25 to 30 mg/kg actual body weight, then 15 to 20 mg/kg IV every 8 to 12 hours, trough 15 to 20 micrograms/mL).

Listeria risk (age over 50, pregnancy, immunosuppression, transplant, malignancy, advanced HIV, diabetes, end-stage kidney disease, cirrhosis, alcohol misuse): add ampicillin 2 g IV loading dose then 2 g IV every 4 hours.

Mild penicillin allergy: meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours plus vancomycin. Severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin plus aztreonam 2 g IV every 6 hours plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg IV every 6 to 8 hours (or vancomycin plus ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 8 hours, levofloxacin 750 mg every 24 hours or moxifloxacin 400 mg every 24 hours, plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days, starting with the first antibiotic dose; stop if another pathogen than Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae type b is identified; not for immunocompromised patients or neuroinvasive listeriosis.
Start aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours if herpes simplex encephalitis is suspected.

Lumbar puncture within 1 hour of arrival (before antibiotics) unless it would delay them; if antibiotics were given first, perform it preferably within 4 hours of starting them. Computed tomography first only for the listed indications.

Intensive care unit criteria: extensive purpura, Glasgow Coma Scale 10 or less or focal signs, brainstem signs, status epilepticus or frequent seizures, shock or instability. Report positive cases to Weqayah; trace close contacts of meningococcal cases for prophylaxis (agent not stated in the MOH protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage
actions: After senior review, urgent non-contrast computed tomography of the head for unexplained thunderclap headache; most accurate within 6 hours of onset.

Blood on the scan: diagnose subarachnoid haemorrhage, offer computed tomography angiography without delay, and urgently discuss transfer with a specialist neurosurgical centre; do not use a severity score alone to decide transfer; rebleeding risk is highest within 24 hours.

Negative scan within 6 hours: do not routinely offer lumbar puncture; consider other diagnoses and seek senior and specialist advice. Negative scan after 6 hours: consider lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset; xanthochromia on spectrophotometry confirms.
Give effective pain relief including opioids if needed and document pupils and neurology allowing for opioid effects.

Nimodipine 60 mg orally, by nasogastric or gastric tube every 4 hours for 21 days, starting within 96 hours of onset (30 mg every 4 hours in cirrhosis); never intravenously from capsule contents; NICE advises intravenous nimodipine only in a specialist setting when enteral is unsuitable.

Manage blood pressure per the NICE hypertension guideline (no target stated in NG228); venous thromboembolism prevention per NICE; do not withhold antiplatelets or anticoagulants solely because of the haemorrhage once the culprit aneurysm is secured.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected giant cell arteritis
actions: Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately if strongly suspected; take full blood count, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate before or immediately after the first dose.

No visual symptoms: prednisolone 40 to 60 mg orally once daily. Acute or intermittent visual loss: methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g IV daily for up to 3 consecutive days (if not immediately available, start oral steroid without delay).
Specialist review the same working day if possible and within 3 working days; new visual loss or double vision needs an ophthalmologist the same calendar day.
Confirm with temporal artery biopsy of at least 1 cm or ultrasound; taper over 12 to 18 months if no relapse; tocilizumab may be considered for high steroid-toxicity risk or relapse.

clinicalManagement.title: Signs of acute narrow-angle glaucoma
actions: Painful red eye with headache is a NICE red flag: arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment (no Saudi or NICE treatment steps were captured).

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnose the primary headache (only after red flags are excluded)
actions: Apply ICHD-3 criteria for migraine, tension-type or cluster headache; keep a headache diary for at least 8 weeks; do not order neuroimaging solely for reassurance.
Aura is suspected with fully reversible symptoms developing over at least 5 minutes and lasting 5 to 60 minutes; investigate or refer for atypical aura.
Menstrual migraine: confirm with a diary over at least 2 cycles.

clinicalManagement.title: Acute treatment by headache type
actions: Migraine, mild to moderate: paracetamol 1,000 mg every 4 hours (maximum 4,000 mg per day), or ibuprofen 400 mg every 4 hours (maximum 2,400 mg per day), or aspirin 650 mg every 4 hours (maximum 4,000 mg per day), or naproxen sodium 500 to 550 mg twice daily, or diclofenac 50 mg once daily; NICE combines an oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol.

Migraine, moderate to severe: sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously (may repeat after 1 hour) or 50 to 100 mg orally once (maximum 200 mg per day); metoclopramide 10 mg IV; ketorolac 30 mg IV or 60 mg IM. Antiemetic: metoclopramide 10 mg or ondansetron 4 to 8 mg twice daily.

Tension-type headache: paracetamol 650 mg every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 g per day) or ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg three to four times daily (maximum 1,200 mg per day) or aspirin 1,000 mg per day; do not offer opioids.

Cluster headache: oxygen 100% by non-rebreather mask at 12 litres per minute or more for 15 minutes, or sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously (maximum 12 mg per day); do not offer paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans.

Menstrual migraine when standard treatment is inadequate: frovatriptan 2.5 mg (second dose after 2 hours for recurrence; maximum 7.5 mg per day) or zolmitriptan 2.5 mg two to three times daily from 2 days before to 5 days after menses onset.

clinicalManagement.title: Prophylaxis
actions: Migraine: propranolol 20 mg two to three times daily increasing weekly to a maximum of 320 mg per day, or topiramate 25 mg in the evening increasing by 25 mg per day to a maximum of 100 mg per day, or amitriptyline 10 to 25 mg at night titrated weekly to a maximum of 150 mg per day, or valproate 250 mg twice daily increasing to 1,000 to 2,000 mg per day (not for women who are pregnant or of childbearing potential without effective contraception), or verapamil 80 mg three times daily to a maximum of 480 mg per day; allow 5 to 8 weeks for effect.

Review the need for prophylaxis at 6 months; chronic tension-type headache: amitriptyline 10 to 25 mg at night titrated to a maximum of 150 mg per day, or up to 10 acupuncture sessions over 5 to 8 weeks.

clinicalManagement.title: Medication-overuse headache
actions: Stop all overused acute drugs abruptly for at least 1 month; warn that headache may worsen short term; review 4 to 8 weeks after withdrawal starts; consider prophylaxis for the underlying headache; do not routinely offer inpatient withdrawal.
MOH acute-treatment day limits for tension-type headache: butalbital-containing 3 days a month, combination analgesics 9 days a month, NSAIDs 15 days a month.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition and follow-up
actions: Admit and involve neurosurgery for subarachnoid haemorrhage; admit with intensive care unit review for meningitis; same-day specialist for giant cell arteritis or glaucoma.
Primary headache with normal examination: explain the diagnosis, give written information, discharge with diary and medication-overuse warning; re-refer if any red flag appears.
Reassess meningitis response at 48 to 72 hours; repeat lumbar puncture for no response after 48 hours of appropriate therapy or unexplained deterioration.

regimens.indication: Empirical treatment of community acute bacterial meningitis, adult under 50 without penicillin allergy
regimens.dose: 2 g
regimens.frequency: Every 12 hours (cefotaxime 2 g IV every 4 to 6 hours is the alternative); always with vancomycin
regimens.duration: Total course by pathogen: 10 to 14 days unspecified or penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus; 5 to 7 days penicillin-susceptible meningococcus; 7 to 10 days beta-lactamase-negative Haemophilus influenzae; 14 to 21 days Streptococcus agalactiae; 21 days Listeria; 21 to 28 days gram-negative and Pseudomonas
adjustments: Renal dosing is deferred by the MOH protocol to the MOH formulary.
Tailor to culture, polymerase chain reaction and susceptibility with infectious diseases and clinical pharmacy.
monitoring: Neurological checks, vital signs and repeat laboratory tests; reassess response within 48 to 72 hours; repeat lumbar puncture if no response at 48 hours.
contraindications: Severe penicillin allergy: use the alternative regimens (contraindication to ceftriaxone itself is not stated in the protocol; check product information).

regimens.dose: Migraine: 6 mg subcutaneously (repeat after 1 hour) or 50 to 100 mg orally once. Cluster: 6 mg at onset
regimens.frequency: Migraine: subcutaneous may repeat once in 1 hour
adjustments: Maximum 200 mg per day orally in migraine; 12 mg per day in cluster headache.
A triptan or paracetamol is listed for pregnancy; the MOH pregnancy triptan entry is garbled and a dose is not given. NICE: consider a triptan only after weighing risks.
contraindications: Ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraine.
Another 5-HT1 agonist or an ergot within 24 hours; monoamine oxidase A inhibitor within 2 weeks.
Hepatic contraindications are listed by the protocol for sumatriptan; check product information.

regimens.indication: Menstrual migraine prophylaxis around menses
regimens.dose: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg (second dose after 2 hours for recurrence); zolmitriptan 2.5 mg; naratriptan 1 mg
regimens.frequency: Frovatriptan: maximum 7.5 mg per day; zolmitriptan 2 to 3 times daily from 2 days before to 5 days after menses onset; naratriptan twice daily starting 2 to 3 days before expected onset for 5 to 6 days
adjustments: Naratriptan contraindicated with creatinine clearance below 15 mL/min.
Zolmitriptan: severe renal dysfunction is a contraindication; contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
contraindications: Ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraine; another 5-HT1 agonist or ergot within 24 hours; monoamine oxidase A inhibitor within 2 weeks; hepatic contraindications for naratriptan.

regimens.indication: Migraine prophylaxis (level A)
regimens.dose: 20 mg twice to three times daily, increased weekly
regimens.duration: Allow 5 to 8 weeks; review need at 6 months (NICE)
adjustments: Maximum 320 mg per day.
Renal and hepatic dose adjustment is not stated in the source opened; check the MOH formulary and product information.

regimens.indication: Migraine prophylaxis (level A); cluster headache prophylaxis
regimens.dose: Migraine: 25 mg in the evening, increased by 25 mg per day. Cluster: 25 mg daily for 7 days then 25 mg weekly increments
regimens.frequency: Evening dose; divided twice daily at higher doses
regimens.duration: Allow 5 to 8 weeks; review at 6 months
adjustments: Maximum 100 mg per day in migraine; 200 mg per day in cluster.
Pregnancy: not for women of childbearing potential unless pregnancy prevention conditions are met (NICE and SIGN; not stated by MOH).
Renal and hepatic dose adjustment is not stated in the source opened; check the MOH formulary and product information.
monitoring: Metabolic acidosis (the protocol notes caution with metformin).
contraindications: Metabolic acidosis with metformin (MOH); pregnancy without prevention conditions.

regimens.indication: Migraine prophylaxis (level A) and cluster headache prophylaxis
regimens.dose: Migraine: 80 mg three times daily increased to a maximum of 480 mg per day. Cluster: 360 to 480 mg per day (the cluster schedule in the extract is garbled)
regimens.duration: Cluster bout; migraine review at 6 months
adjustments: NICE: seek specialist advice before cluster use including electrocardiogram monitoring.
monitoring: Electrocardiogram, heart rate and blood pressure.
contraindications: Severe left ventricular dysfunction, hypotension, sick sinus syndrome, second- or third-degree atrioventricular block.

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from the MOH Headache Disorder protocol (undated) unless the source line states otherwise; meningitis doses are from the MOH 2025 meningitis protocol; nimodipine and giant cell arteritis doses are from the secondary sources named. Where the MOH protocol gives no renal, hepatic or pregnancy advice for a drug, that gap is stated and the MOH formulary or product information must be checked.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: At least 5 attacks; 4 to 72 hours untreated; at least 2 of unilateral, pulsating, moderate or severe intensity, aggravated by routine activity; at least 1 of nausea and/or vomiting, or photophobia and phonophobia; not better explained by another diagnosis.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Frequent episodic tension-type headache (ICHD-3, as paraphrased by the source page)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: At least 10 episodes, on 1 to 14 days a month for more than 3 months; 30 minutes to 7 days; at least 2 of bilateral, pressing or tightening, mild or moderate, not aggravated by routine activity; no nausea or vomiting; at most 1 of photophobia or phonophobia.

At least 5 attacks; severe or very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes untreated; ipsilateral autonomic sign or restlessness; frequency from one every other day to 8 a day.
Headache on 15 or more days per month for more than 3 months with migraine features.
Non-contrast CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset; lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset if CT is negative after 6 hours.
First dose within 1 hour of hospital presentation; results of cerebrospinal fluid testing within 4 hours of lumbar puncture.
Stop overused drugs for at least 1 month; review 4 to 8 weeks after withdrawal starts.

guidelineComparison.title: Where the Saudi MOH headache protocol and NICE CG150 differ

values: Listed: dihydroergotamine 1 mg IV with metoclopramide; ergotamine 1 to 4 mg then 1 to 2 mg every 30 minutes, maximum 6 mg per attack or 10 mg per week. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
Level B: up to 1,200 mg per day.
650 mg every 4 hours, maximum 4,000 mg per day.
400 mg every 4 hours, maximum 2,400 mg per day.
Oral triptans are not offered for acute cluster treatment; the extract also lists zolmitriptan 1 mg for cluster, which conflicts and is not given here.
Do not offer oral triptans for cluster headache.

guidelineComparison.note: Shown side by side and not merged; follow the Saudi MOH protocol and the local neurology advice where they differ.

teaching.scope: Adult with headache presenting to the emergency department or primary care: immediate recognition and management of life-threatening secondary headache (subarachnoid haemorrhage, bacterial meningitis and meningoencephalitis, giant cell arteritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma), then diagnosis and drug treatment of migraine, tension-type and cluster headache, using Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) protocols with named international guidance where the Saudi documents are silent. Adults only.
learningObjectives: Recognise the red flags that mean a secondary headache.
Start meningitis antibiotics within 1 hour and image subarachnoid haemorrhage within 6 hours.
Diagnose primary headaches with ICHD-3 and treat by type.
pitfalls: Delaying antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture.
Giving oral triptans or NSAIDs for cluster headache.
Prescribing valproate or topiramate to women of childbearing potential without prevention measures.
keyPoints: Thunderclap headache: CT within 6 hours; lumbar puncture only at least 12 hours after onset.
Meningitis: blood cultures, then antibiotics within 1 hour; never delay for imaging.
Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days, never intravenous from capsules.
Giant cell arteritis: start steroid on suspicion, same-day specialist.

patientEducation: Return immediately for sudden severe headache, fever with neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, visual loss or a painful red eye.
Keep a headache diary and limit acute pain medicine days.
Take acute migraine treatment early in the attack.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular sleep, meals and hydration; identify triggers with the diary.
mdtReferrals: Emergency medicine; neurology; neurosurgery; infectious diseases; ophthalmology; rheumatology; clinical pharmacy; intensive care.
dischargeCriteria: Discharge only when red flags are excluded and the examination is normal; provide diary, medication-overuse warning and return advice.
Meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage and giant cell arteritis are not discharged from the emergency department without specialist plan.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Primary headache: review at 6 months for prophylaxis and 4 to 8 weeks after medication withdrawal; meningitis: reassess at 48 to 72 hours; giant cell arteritis: specialist follow-up with taper over 12 to 18 months.
